#721. Milcho Manchevski’s ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’ Wins Top Prize at Tokyo Film Fest

Macedonian filmmaker examination of families and the wealth gap takes Grand Prix and brings 10 days of festival to a close.

Milcho Manchevski’s Sister Brother Manhole Cover took the Grand Prix at Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF), as the event closed as it had opened, on a rainy day in the Japanese capital.

The Macedonian filmmaker’s winner tells of fraternal and maternal love on the edges of society, in his first feature since Kaymak, which was also in competition in Tokyo, in 2022. The prize comes with the Governor of Tokyo Award’s $19,000 (3 million yen). The two leads Sara Klimoska and Filip Trajkovikj were in attendance, along with producer Kortoshev, who accepted the award in place of Manchevski, who had left Tokyo but sent a video message. Related Stories TV Tony Awards to Air on CBS Through 2032 Movies AFM: Dark Sky Takes 'American Dollhouse' for U.S. (Exclusive)

The best director award went to Argentina’s Lisandro Alonso for Double Freedom. The special jury prize was won by Magic Atlas by Sun Xun, which took more than a decade to complete, and became the first animation selected for the main competition in Tokyo. Hu Ling won best actress for The Night That Binds Us, a France-Hong Kong co-production, while Japan’s only win came in the form of Narita Ryo’s best actor for Two Cigarettes, Three Nights.

The jury was headed by Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer, alongside producers Alex Lo and Oh Jungwan, actor Watanabe Makiko and colorist Yov Moor.

Heysel 85, set against the backdrop of the Heysel Stadium disaster that killed 39 supporters during the 1985 European Cup Final between Liverpool and Juventus, won the audience award for director Teodora Ana Mihai.

Serife Tavsan, by Afghani director Tareq Daoud, won the Asian Future competition for emerging regional filmmakers and a $6,325 (1 million yen) cash prize.

More than 69,000 people attended screenings of 204 films during the 10 days of the 39th edition of the festival across the Hibiya-Marunouchi-Yurakucho-Ginza area, up slightly on last year.

#720. Texas’ New Attorney General Nathan Johnson Is a Former ‘Dragon Ball Z’ Composer

Johnson composed the musical scores for 67 episodes and five movies.

The Blue Wave that swept through Texas this week also has some Dragon Ball Z energy.

Nathan Johnson, a veteran litigator and Texas state senator, was elected this week as attorney general of the Lone Star State, assuming the role in January 2027.

Johnson lists swimming, reading “boring books,” and making peanut butter as his guilty pleasures, but his interest in the popular anime television series Dragon Ball Z became an early career move. Explore Billboard See latest videos, charts and news

“If you grew up watching Dragon Ball Z, you might know me better than you think: I composed the musical scores for 67 episodes and five movies, and had a great time doing it,” he writes on his Facebook page. Chojo' as Vaundy's 'Shiwaawase' Reaches Top 3 Tinashe Sends Message to Republican Fans During 2026 Midterm Elections: 'Y'all Can Go'

Those “wall to wall” scores were cut in the 2000s and include Dragon Ball Z: The World’s Strongest, Dragon Ball Z: The Tree of Might, Dragon Ball Z: Broly — Second Coming, Dragon Ball Z: Fusion Reborn and Dragon Ball Z: Wrath of the Dragon.

“It was a lot of fun,” Johnson recounts in a video posted in June. “I had a one-year-old at the time, and I remember him sitting on my knee and stuff blowing up. He was like ‘oh, daddy, Goku,’” he continued, identifying the show’s lead character.

“He just thought it was super cool. Even then it just gave me street cred with my kids’ friends and it gave me a creative outlet and a cultural connection that very few people had the opportunity to have.”

Created by Akira Toriyama and produced by Toei Animation, Dragon Ball Z is a sci-fi fantasy that follows the adventures of Goku, an alien warrior. The anime premiered in 1989 in Japan and was syndicated in the United States on Cartoon Network from 1998 until 2008. Its celebrity fans include Kendrick Lamar, Steve Aoki, Bad Bunny, Big Sean and Anuel AA.

The multihyphenate Johnson holds a B.S. in physics from the University of Arizona and a law degree from the University of Texas at Austin, and took office in 2019. Since then, he has authored at least 433 bills and more than 130 into law.

Johnson won the Texas attorney general election on Wednesday, Nov. 3 as the Democrats routed the Republicans in the midterms, seizing control of the Senate and the House of Representatives. On the way to an historic victory, the Dems flipped seven Senate seats, nearly 30 House districts, five governorships and up to 12 state legislative chambers.

#719. Nithya Raman Projected to Win Los Angeles Mayor’s Race, Defeating Karen Bass

The city councilmember, who represents an industry-heavy district, ran an insurgent progressive campaign against the city's Democratic Party machine, unseating troubled incumbent Bass. One respected outlet has called the race.

Nithya Raman is projected to be the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, according to one outlet, unseating incumbent Karen Bass, a fellow Democrat who struggled with credibility as constituent anger surged over various municipal ills, including housing and affordability, the entertainment production exodus and her response to the Palisades wildfire. A win for the leftist City Councilmember, running as an outsider against the local party machine, would be a significant victory for the region’s progressive movement, which heavily skews toward younger voters who rent instead of owning their homes. Related Stories News Best Memes and TikToks After Midterms' Blue Wave, From Regina George to 'The Office' References Midterms 2026 DNC Vice Chair: "We Had to Hit the Bottom"

Independent election polling site Decision Desk H.Q., which partners with Ballotpedia, announced it was projecting a Raman victory, though other major entities such as NBC News had yet to call the race. Raman is currently up more than three percent, with nearly three-quarters of expected votes now tallied. The full count may not be in for a week or longer, as any mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day are still valid even if they arrive by early next week.

During her election night party on Nov. 3 at the Greek Theatre in Griffith Park, Raman denounced the “cynicism” which “started to make us believe that L.A.’s problems weren’t just bad, but they were permanent.” She avowed that the city “is worth fighting for every single day of our lives.”

Raman, 45, is a Harvard- and MIT-trained urban planner who founded a L.A. homelessness nonprofit and served as executive director of Time’s Up, the ill-fated advocacy organization focused on workplace sexual harassment, before winning her City Council seat in 2020. The industry-heavy district spans the southern swath of the San Fernando Valley, from Sherman Oaks to Studio City, across the Hollywood Hills to the Eastside enclaves of Los Feliz and Silver Lake. It includes the Hollywood Bowl, the Hollywood Sign and NBCUniversal.

Through each of her campaigns, Raman, who was born in India and will be the city’s first Asian American mayor, has generated Hollywood support — particularly from its TV comedy scene. Donors to her mayoral race have included Tina Fey, Mike Schur, Mindy Kaling and Cord Jefferson. She’s married to Vali Chandrasekaran, a writer-producer who has worked on 30 Rock, Modern Family, My Name is Earl and The Four Seasons. (They have twin 10-year-old children.)

During their campaigns, both candidates said they’d back unlimited film and TV credits at the state level, and champion a federal tax incentive to make the U.S. more internationally competitive. Raman has attacked Bass’ handling of the issue, including her tardiness in appointing a film liaison to the industry. Still, despite her closeness to the industry, Raman’s record of advocating for Hollywood’s needs has been called into question, even as the city and state continued to experience its historic runaway production. (The effects of the entertainment free fall have been felt across the local economy.)

In office, Raman’s key policy focus has been on housing, first championing Measure ULA, known as the “Mansion Tax,” then criticizing the unintended consequences of the legislation once its ruinous impact on apartment construction became clear. She’s since pushed for reform. (The issue has been a recurring subplot on Netflix’s real-life drama about L.A. real estate, Selling Sunset.)

Bass, 73, was Los Angeles’ first female mayor and second Black mayor. A former community organizer turned veteran elected official, she spent years ascending to the top of California’s state assembly before spending more than a decade in Congress, representing a largely African American and Hispanic section of South L.A., which has been her political base. Joe Biden reportedly took her under serious consideration to be his running mate while he was the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee in 2020.

Bass has long maintained Hollywood ties. Her most prominent supporters in her mayoral reelection campaign included Jane Fonda, J.J. Abrams, Samuel L. Jackson and Anthony Anderson.

Raman ran to the left of Bass. Her campaign included a sit-down interview with the controversial leftist streamer Hasan Piker, as well as a fraught relationship with the Democratic Socialists of America. Once a dues-paying member of the organization’s local chapter, citing its commitment to housing affordability, she was censured by DSA L.A. in 2024 for not fully adopting its policy positions against Israel. In the mayoral race, the local chapter ultimately backed her, while the DSA’s national leadership challenged that endorsement.

Raman’s last-minute insurgent run against the local Democratic Party machine put her at odds with a bloc of her fellow progressives on the City Council, who had already endorsed Bass. The top sitting L.A. politicians to endorse her were County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, who considered her own run against Bass and represents a swath of the Westside affected by the Palisades wildfire, along with the City Controller Kenneth Mejia. Now Raman, Mejia and newly elected L.A. City Attorney Marissa Roy, who’s a member of the DSA, constitute a triumvirate of progressivism at the highest reaches of City Hall.

The general election followed a heated primary race defined by the reactionary-populist run of the former reality TV star Spencer Pratt. He drew national attention for his high-energy campaign of grievance politics after he lost his house during the Palisades wildfire due to what he argued was government negligence.

Another key figure through the cycle has been the local billionaire real estate developer Rick Caruso, a center-right Democrat who lost to Bass in 2022. He declined to run again but has remained a prominent and influential presence in the city’s political conversation. Despite having fiercely criticized Bass during her term, including over her handling of the Palisades disaster (his own Palisades Village luxury shopping center was damaged), he announced in October that he would be voting for her.

Raman’s term will overlap with L.A.’s hosting of the 2028 Summer Olympics, a global spectacle offering the city an opportunity to reboot its tarnished image. The former Lucasfilm head Kathleen Kennedy recently took the baton to oversee the ceremonies after Peter Rice, who had been running the effort, became Netflix’s chief content officer.

No one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. It arrived with excellent timing on Halloween, which made the already-creepy asteroid even creepier.

During its closest approach, the creepy asteroid was about 300,000 miles from Earth, or 1.3 times the average distance between Earth and the moon. So, it didn't pose a threat to our planet. It was discovered by astronomers at Hawaii's Pan-STARRS observatory only three weeks before the flyby, and it was given the official designation "2015 TB145." But no one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.

NASA called the asteroid the "Great Pumpkin," while others called it the "Halloween Asteroid."

Be afraid, be very afraid... Okay, not really, but there is reason to be concerned about near-Earth objects and the time in which they are detected.

"According to the catalog of near-Earth objects (NEOs) kept by the Minor Planet Center, this is the closest currently known approach by an object this large until asteroid 1999 AN10, at about 2,600 feet (800 meters) in size, approaches at about 1 lunar distance (238,000 miles from Earth) in August 2027," NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) reported in 2015.

NASA’s Near-Earth Object Observations Program, sometimes called “Spaceguard,” works to catalog these type of objects and predicts some of their paths if they could be potentially threats to our planet. While there are no known credible impact threats to date, it doesn't mean the "Great Pumpkin," or rather a great impactor, isn't real.

As for 2015 TB145, it did return to Earth's vicinity in 2018, but at a much more distant pass of about 24 million miles (38 million kilometers), "or about a quarter the distance between Earth and the sun," according to JPL.

#717. Russia in Africa: What is Putin hoping to achieve?

Following its invasion of Ukraine and the resulting rift with the West, Russia has declared that it intends to make a "historic return" to Africa. What have we seen of this so far?

The conflict with the West sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine  prompted Russian President Vladimir Putin to seek support from other parts of the world. Africa has become a focus, with foreign minister Sergei Lavrov visiting the continent increasingly often.

Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova has described it as a "historic return," and declared no one and nothing could be compared to what Russia did for Africa in the 20th century.

A Russia-Africa summit has been held in Russia at roughly three-year intervals since 2019. The third takes place in Moscow on October 28 and 29. The program focusses on economic cooperation. Other topics range from politics and security to science and culture. But Russia is actively working with only a few African countries, mainly in the north of the continent, and this is reflected in the trade figures.

"South Africa is still Africa's largest national economy, but its volume of trade with Russia is small, far less than with Egypt and Algeria," says Ivan Klyszcz from the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Tallinn, Estonia.

"Egypt and Algeria in particular are key partners for Russia. Egypt plays an important role in this regard. Russian diplomats and business representatives are trying to extend relationships with other countries, especially Tanzania and Ethiopia, but with no appreciable success so far."

Egypt is the second-largest economy in Africa, and the bilateral volume of trade with Russia has more than doubled since 2021; in 2025, according to Russia's Federal Customs Service, it was $10.5 billion (€9.4 billion). Consignments of Russian grain are the main drivers, followed by products of the metal industry. Egypt's exports to Russia are primarily fruit and vegetables.

There are investment projects, too. Russia is building a big nuclear power plant in the Egyptian region of El-Dabaa on the Mediterranean coast. Construction is being financed by a Russian loan of 25 billion US dollars, which covers around 85% of the costs.

Egypt is one of the few African countries with which Russia enjoys stable business relationships, as well as having extensive experience of cooperation, says Nikita Smagin, an expert on Russian policy in the Middle East. "In the long term, Egypt could become Moscow's gateway to Africa and to other markets," he says. "But Cairo is pursuing its own interests. It would be too optimistic to hope that Egypt is lending its support purely out of political solidarity."

According to the Russian customs service, around 39% of Russian–African trade in 2025 was with Egypt, and total sales between Russia and all 54 countries of the African continent came to around 27 billion US dollars. Africa's share of Russia's foreign trade is therefore very small (3.9% in 2025), and not at all commensurate with the attention Moscow is devoting to its relations with African countries.

Russia is not a significant trading partner for Africa, either. The most important partner for African countries is the European Union. In 2025, the volume of trade with the EU came to around 385 billion US dollars. African countries' statistics also show that other partners were well ahead of Russia. The volume of trade with China was in excess of 348 billion US dollars in 2025; with the United States it was almost 105 billion, and 103 billion with India.

Fidel Owusu, a Ghanaian expert with Geopolitical Intelligence Services (GIS) in Liechtenstein, comments that Russia's economic presence in Africa has not been as significant as that of China, the United States, India, or other traditional powers like France and Britain. "If you look at the volume of trade and the kind of investment," he says, "in recent times, some middle powers such as Turkey and the UAW are doing far better than Russia."

Beverly Ochieng, a senior analyst with Control Risks, a global risk and strategic intelligence consultancy in Senegal, observes: "Western countries continue to dominate in strategically important areas such as raw material extraction, finance, and the energy sector, even if their political presence in the region is declining." According to her, "Russia will compete more intensively for access to critical mineral resources and energy projects. We see this with lithium projects in Mali as well as with nuclear power initiatives across the continent."

Russia's presence in Africa is more obvious in the military sector than in the fields of trade and investment. Starting with the arrival of the Wagner Group, Russian mercenaries have been supporting African regimes, particularly those of the unstable countries in the Sahel region. In exchange, their associated subsidiaries are granted access to raw materials. Following the death of the Wagner Group leader, Yevgeny Prigozhin, most of these operations were taken over by the Africa Corps, a paramilitary group set up and controlled by Russia's defense ministry.

According to the Congressional Research Service, the think tank of the US Congress, the largest Russian military contingents, each comprising several thousand men, are in the Central African Republic, Mali, and Libya. The Africa Corps is also keen to extend its presence in Burkina Faso and Niger. Russian mercenaries have also been spotted in Equatorial Guinea.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Irina Filatova from the University of Cape Town stresses that there are several reasons why it's important for Russia to maintain a military presence in Africa. "The countries have sizeable deposits of minerals such as gold and uranium. Through them, it's possible to exert influence over Europe's southern borders, including in matters of migration and regional security. With regard to Libya, the country is an important logistical hub for connections with the Sahel and central Africa. Goods can easily be supplied via Libya to countries without access to the sea," Filatova says.

Ultimately, Russia is still one of the biggest suppliers of arms to African countries, even though Russian exports have fallen over the course of the war in Ukraine. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates Moscow's share of the African market for the years 2021–2025 at 15%, which puts it in third place behind the United States (19%) and China (17%). Between 2020 and 2024, its share was even higher: It was in first place with 21%, followed by China with 18%, and the US with 16%.

Ivan Klyszcz from the ICDS says that while Russia is not a significant economic partner for Africa, the fact that it supplies food and fertilizer and has a military presence in some countries means that Moscow's influence in Africa is far greater than is suggested by the volume of trade and investment alone.

"I believe Russia sees the diplomatic weight of Africa," says Fidel Owusu. "When I talk of diplomatic weight, I mean numbers – the continent has the largest number of countries. Russia wants that kind of support in the UN General Assembly whenever votes are cast. In recent times it has done better than in earlier votes."

In recent years, Russia has been positioning itself on the international stage as representing the interests of the Global South.

"We want to work with Africa, we are working with Africa and we will continue to do so. But our aim is not, as it was for the colonial powers, to make money or steal something from Africa, but to develop together," Russian president Vladimir Putin said recently at a conference of the Moscow-based Valdai Discussion Club.

References to the colonial past appeal to some countries but not others, says Irina Filatova. "Africa is not a country, it's a continent. There are differences in the perception of Russia, as well as in the way Russia positions itself. Also, the views of the political elites are often substantially different from those of ordinary citizens. In South Africa, for instance, the Russian narrative is received very positively. An anti-colonial agenda is also popular in other countries, but it isn't necessarily associated with Russia."

Antonio Cascais contributed to this report. It was originally written in Russian.

#716. Six Hollywood Consequences of Tuesday’s Democrat Blockbuster

From the federal tax credit to cable-news trolling to AI regulation, the world looks a lot different today than it did last week before the election.

The massive showing by Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections impacts everyone who lives in this country. But the entertainment industry has a particular role, given its charge to tell stories — to explain America to itself. And now there’s suddenly a whole new chapter to write about a country that has decided to radically reject the politics of many of the past ten years.But man, that sounds awfully high-minded. There are far more concrete examples. Here are six entertainment realms that could look a lot different after Tuesday’s domination.Bring on the film money?The federal film tax credit had a little bit of momentum with Republican lawmakers like Tim Scott, Brian Jack and Nathaniel Moran and Democrats such as Adam Schiff, Laura Friedman and Linda Sanchez introducing a bill last month to establish the 20 percent credit for certain labor costs. Where does Tuesday leave it? Well, the good news is all the lead champions in Congress have won re-election and will be back to work next session (though Scott may have to spend a few extra minutes in the morning wiping egg off his face for his “unequivocal” assertion that Republicans would maintain Senate control).The question is whether they can rally enough fellow lawmakers behind it. On paper, Republicans would want to join the cause, as it’s a win for them at a time when those won’t be easy to come by. Doubly so for President Donald Trump, who will be eager to crow about…something, and bringing some jobs back to the U.S. will allow for the chirp.The snag is that the tax credit reduces the U.S. tax base at a time of massive deficits and when many Democrats are promising a restoration of benefits — i.e., the kind of thing you need a deep tax base for. Supporters will argue this is tax revenue that wouldn’t have happened anyway if production was going overseas (sometimes but not always true) and that it will benefit workers (yes, will trickle down, but the actual rebate goes to producers, some of the bigger of whom won’t be seen as needing a handout). On paper this should still have a decent shot. But Congressional turnovers can mess with priorities. Put this in the unknown column.Texas artists saw it all alongNo one around the cable-news dial could quite believe that Texas had elected a Democratic senator for the first time in 38 years or governor for the first time in 32. Harry Enten was so in disbelief he almost got into a fight with his accent.We should have paid closer attention to creatives. They’ve been telling us how it’s possible — telling us of another Texas — all along. Natalie Maines of the (then-Dixie) Chicks famously and at the expense of her career told a London audience at the start of the Iraq War in 2003 that “we do not want this war, this violence. And we’re ashamed that the president of the United States is from Texas.”But it’s been creeping in plenty of other Texas artists’ work too — in the films of Richard Linklater and his anti-exploitation 2006 movie Fast Food Nation and the arched eyebrow-to-false-jingoism Last Flag Flying in 2017. Mike Judge, pushing back against George W. Bush-era compliance in 2006’s retroactive documentary Idiocracy. Or even just the work of an Austinite like David Modigliani and his 2019 nonfiction piece Running with Beto. (Actually, Beto walked so James Talarico could run.) We haven’t always paid attention.No doubt we’ll soon start hearing other artists around the country tell us a place is a lot more Democratic than its Republican politicians want to project. After Tuesday, it’s worth listening.Anti-media trollingYou know how you’re going for some minor medical procedure and the doctor’s like, “In the short term, it will hurt like hell, but then you’ll feel a lot better?”I suspect we’ll get a whole lash-out at mainstream media figures by Trump and members of his administration after Tuesday’s drubbing. “Outlets are failing,” “hosts should be fired,” you know the lyrics. But lame ducks tend to get lamer as their term wears on, and once Trump sees how little effect this is having — the meager few days of Jimmy Kimmel suspension he got after the Charlie Kirk joke last year will practically look like a Colbert canning by comparison — I suspect we’ll start seeing a lower-key approach or just his attention turned elsewhere.Spasms from the FCC are still possible, Brendan Carr writing letters to this media company or not asking them to drop by for a not-so-friendly visit. But how hard do you want to go when — oh yes, you’re not a presidential cabinet department but an agency overseen and funded by….Congress? The Carr witch hunts and saber rattles of the past two years are going to get a lot quieter. Who knows? Maybe the media companies will stop quaking in their boots and even restore a DEI program or two.David Ellison’s true colorsFor months we’ve been told by Ellison apologists — and David Ellison — that the new owner of Warner Bros. wasn’t actually a Trumper; he just played one at UFC fights. Ellison needed Trump to get his deals through, so it was all realpolitik. Well, now he doesn’t need that — in fact, if anything, a Trump association hurts him with a new Congress. So does he reveal himself to be the pragmatist his defenders say (or even the liberal on many issues that he says he is)? Or, with his Trump cover falling away, does he just unmask as the conservative he’s been up all along? First test up is Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, coming in a few months from HBO. Does he still release it despite its targeting of the leading GOP donor? Musk just paid a lot of money to Skydance, potentially so HBO doesn’t air it, though he has bigger challenges to worry about right now. Related Stories Midterms 2026 Nithya Raman Projected to Win Los Angeles Mayor's Race, Defeating Karen Bass News Best Memes and TikToks After Midterms' Blue Wave, From Regina George to 'The Office' References

And there will be all sorts of other markers — films to buy, TV shows to air, news divisions to revamp — for one of the bigger moguls operating today. We’ll see what he’s really made of soon enough. At the very least John Oliver could rest a little easier today. Speaking of Musk, and getting things right, Alex Gibney’s idea that if we just pull back the curtain his weakness will be revealed was practically born out in lockstep on Tuesday as Musk’s half a billion went for naught. “The Great and Terrible Oz kept people in check because they were afraid of his visage that loomed over everybody, and he used that power to exert an enormous amount of control,” Gibney told THR last month. “But when a little dog pulled aside the curtain, and you can see a frumpy man operating gears and levers, suddenly he wasn’t so terrible and he wasn’t so great.” Exactly.One loser in all of this: Rob Bonta and the AGs who garnered a…modest settlement from Ellison in his WBD acquisition as pressure mounted from various politicians and leaders. Had the attorneys general just held out six more weeks, they would have had all of Congress and a whole new vibe on their side.

Celebrity…non-activism?The Hollywood model for this electoral season has been really interesting. Many people you talk to around the entertainment business and beyond have said some version of Hollywood sitting this out. But that’s not exactly true. Entertainers lent plenty of financial muscle to these midterms — see under: all the fundraisers thrown by A-listers, from Damon Lindelof for James Talarico to Shonda Rhimes for Jon Ossoff, along with all the donations from the likes of Chuck Lorre, Sally Field and Casey Bloys. Damn, Don Henley alone gave a half-million dollars to various candidates in Texas.

What happened a lot less were public campaign appearances. Celebrities did that nonstop in 2024, and it either didn’t help or got them (and their Democratic candidates) pulverized. If your party’s message is “return power to the people,” then some very rich red-carpet types standing there telling you how to do it sort of jams the signal and generally casts an elitist cloud over your message. We ain’t in 2004 anymore.

No doubt 2028 will bring plenty of big names stumping for candidates. People want to help, and famous people want to help famously; nothing wrong with that. But after the stark contrast between 2024 and now, we might see a different tack. Maybe a candidate doesn’t turn down Beyoncé who wants to show up at a campaign event. But maybe also Beyoncé thinks twice before offering? It’s not like stumping makes celebs’ lives easier either.

One other change: the idea of celebs running for office. A time-honored tradition. But Michele Tafoya just rode her Sunday Night Football popularity to the Republican nomination for Senate in Minnesota — then got trounced by 14 points. I mean, if a celebrity can’t get elected in Minnesota…That said, if McConaughey scratched his political itch and tossed his cowboy hat in the ring for, say, Ted Cruz’s seat in four years, how many of us would object?AI pullbackWhat kind of actual regulation we’ll get on AI remains to be seen. Ed Markey may have promised all those subpoenas for tech executives, and there’s a general air of bring-Big-Tech-in, but actually stopping Silicon Valley from developing new models and products is hard. It would be like trying to stop politicians from issuing press releases — it’s what they do. Also, there’s a pacing misalignment because Congress moves slowly and writes laws and tech companies move fast and write code. Also, tech companies have a lot of money and a lot of lobbyists.All those caveats said, the winds blow differently now. Many of next term’s 259 House Democrats and 54-56 Senate Democrats got there by promising tougher oversight on AI, particularly on data centers, and they’ll be incentivized to make some moves. And even if Trump won’t sign bills of that kind, the numbers are now lopsided enough that Senate Democrats would just need to peel off a few Republicans to get a 60-vote filibuster. (Josh Hawley, John Curtis and John Kennedy of Missouri/Utah/Louisiana come to mind; they’ve all expressed Big Tech-skeptical feelings.)All of this could slow down how quickly the models get developed and thus how fast they get adopted by studios or consumers. Good news for creatives, most of whom are fine with AI as a limited-use tool, less so as a soul- and job-destroying blunt instrument of automation.

#714. Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth

Scientists have discovered that molten rock deep inside Earth can store far more oxygen than previously believed. The finding challenges long-standing assumptions about magma and raises an intriguing possibility: oxygen released from Earth's interior may have helped transform the planet's atmosphere billions of years ago.

Through high-pressure experiments and advanced computer simulations, researchers found that magma can absorb additional oxygen beyond the amount normally required by its chemical composition. This hidden oxygen could provide a previously unrecognized connection between Earth's deep interior, volcanic activity, and the development of an oxygen-rich atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Yanhao Lin and Dr. Ho-kwang Mao of the Center for High Pressure Science and Technology Advanced Research (HPSTAR), working with Prof. Haiyang Niu of Northwestern Polytechnical University and Prof. Wim van Westrenen of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Their findings were published in National Science Review.

Scientists Challenge a Long-Standing Assumption About Magma

Oxygen is one of the most abundant elements inside Earth, accounting for more than half of the atoms in the planet's silicate interior. Silicates are minerals and molten materials composed primarily of silicon and oxygen, along with other elements. They make up much of Earth's mantle and crust.

Despite oxygen's abundance, scientists have traditionally assumed that magma can contain only a specific amount of it. Under this understanding, the oxygen content is determined by the quantities and electrical charge states of other elements in the molten rock, including silicon, magnesium, and iron.

Water and carbon dioxide behave differently. Both can dissolve in magma and later escape as gases when the surrounding pressure decreases. These substances are known as volatile components, and their release plays an important role in volcanic activity.

Oxygen, however, has generally not been treated as a separate volatile substance that magma can absorb and release. Whether molten silicate rock could hold additional oxygen independently of its ordinary chemical composition remained largely unexplored.

The new research suggests that this assumption may need to change.

Extreme Pressure Reveals Hidden Oxygen in Molten Rock

To investigate, the scientists recreated conditions found deep within Earth using laboratory equipment capable of generating extraordinary pressures and temperatures.

They heated a synthetic version of mid-ocean ridge basalt, a type of volcanic rock commonly produced where tectonic plates move apart beneath the oceans. The samples were exposed to pressures ranging from normal atmospheric pressure to 7 gigapascals and temperatures between 1200 and 1800 °C.

A pressure of 7 gigapascals is approximately 69,000 times the atmospheric pressure at Earth's surface.

The team used specialized piston-cylinder and cubic presses to maintain these extreme conditions. They also added platinum oxide (PtO2) to establish an oxygen-rich environment and test how much additional oxygen the molten rock could absorb.

After the experiments, the researchers rapidly cooled the molten material, producing glass that preserved important characteristics of the melt. They then analyzed its elemental composition and measured the amounts of water and carbon dioxide present.

By calculating how much oxygen was needed to balance the other elements, along with the oxygen already contained in water and carbon dioxide, the scientists could estimate how much remained unaccounted for.

They called this additional amount "excess oxygen."

The results revealed a striking relationship between pressure and oxygen storage.

At normal atmospheric pressure, the glass contained almost no excess oxygen. At 7 gigapascals, however, excess oxygen accounted for more than 5% of the sample's weight.

For comparison, experiments conducted at similar pressures and temperatures without added platinum oxide produced excess oxygen concentrations of only 0.2% to 0.5% by weight.

The researchers also wanted to determine whether the additional oxygen was truly incorporated into the material or merely trapped as tiny gas bubbles.

Using Raman spectroscopy, a technique that identifies substances by examining how they interact with light, they found no detectable signature of oxygen gas in the glass. This indicated that the excess oxygen had become part of the glass structure rather than accumulating in bubbles.

The measured concentrations may even underestimate magma's actual oxygen-storage capacity. Some oxygen could have escaped while the molten samples were cooling, meaning the original melts may have contained still greater amounts.

Computer Simulations Reveal How Magma Stores Extra Oxygen

To better understand the discovery at the atomic level, Prof. Niu led a series of theoretical computer simulations.

The researchers used deep neural network (DNN) models to simulate interactions among atoms with accuracy approaching that of ab initio calculations, which describe atomic behavior using fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

The simulations showed that additional oxygen could dissolve into molten material until the system reached equilibrium, a state in which oxygen entering and leaving the melt is balanced.

Although the computer models used a simplified system containing only magnesium, silicon, and oxygen, they reproduced the same overall pattern observed in the laboratory: magma's ability to hold excess oxygen increased with pressure.

The simulated oxygen concentrations were lower than the experimental measurements, which the scientists attributed to differences between the simplified model and the more complex chemical composition of actual basalt.

The calculations also revealed changes in how oxygen atoms behaved as more oxygen entered the melt. Their electrical charges became more varied, and a small proportion formed peroxide-like bonds, in which oxygen atoms bond to one another.

These changes help explain how molten rock might accommodate oxygen beyond the amount predicted by conventional chemical models.

Importantly, the pressure-dependent behavior resembles that of water and carbon dioxide, which also become more soluble in magma as pressure increases.

Based on these findings, the researchers propose that oxygen should be recognized as an independent component of silicate melts, rather than being considered only in relation to other elements.

Could Ancient Volcanoes Have Helped Oxygenate Earth's Atmosphere?

The discovery raises a much larger question about Earth's history: Could magma have transported significant amounts of oxygen from the planet's interior to its surface?

The researchers suggest a possible mechanism involving magma generated in oxidized regions of Earth's mantle.

Under the immense pressures deep underground, this magma could absorb substantial quantities of excess oxygen. As it moves upward, the surrounding pressure decreases, reducing the amount of oxygen the molten rock can retain.

Some of that oxygen could then be released, potentially contributing to chemical reactions that increase the oxidation of the upper mantle, Earth's crust, and eventually the atmosphere.

Oxidation refers to chemical processes involving the transfer of electrons. In this context, oxygen carried by magma could increase the oxidizing capacity of surrounding materials and potentially influence the balance of oxygen in the atmosphere.

This proposed mechanism may also help explain an intriguing coincidence in Earth's geological past.

Between approximately 2.5 billion and 2.0 billion years ago, atmospheric oxygen levels underwent major increases. This interval overlaps with the formation of some of Earth's largest large igneous provinces (LIPs), enormous regions of volcanic rock created by exceptionally large outpourings of magma.

The researchers suggest that oxygen released from these ancient volcanic systems could have contributed to changes in atmospheric composition.

Their preliminary calculation highlights the potentially enormous scale of the process. They estimate that if magma erupted during this period released excess oxygen equal to just 0.27% of its weight, the total amount could theoretically match all the oxygen present in Earth's atmosphere today.

This does not establish that volcanic activity actually supplied that much atmospheric oxygen. Instead, it illustrates how even a relatively small release of oxygen from immense quantities of magma could have major planetary consequences.

A New Clue to Earth's Evolution and Habitable Planets

The findings could influence several important areas of planetary science.

For one, they may change how scientists understand ancient magma oceans, vast regions of molten rock believed to have existed during the early evolution of Earth and other rocky planets.

They also introduce a possible new factor in volcanic degassing, the process through which gases and other volatile substances escape from molten rock and interact with a planet's atmosphere.

If magma can store and release oxygen independently of its other chemical components, models of Earth's atmospheric development may need to account for this previously overlooked process.

The implications could extend beyond Earth. Understanding how oxygen moves between the interiors and atmospheres of rocky planets may help researchers investigate the conditions that allow potentially habitable environments to develop and persist over billions of years.

Although further research is needed to establish how much oxygen natural magmas carry and how much reaches the atmosphere, the discovery points to a surprising possibility: some of the processes that helped shape Earth's oxygen-rich environment may have originated far beneath the planet's surface.

#713. The Top 26 Looks in 2026 (So Far), According to 50 of Hollywood’s Biggest Stylists

The Hollywood Reporter presents its inaugural data-driven stylists’ survey, in which tastemakers voted on their peers’ most impressive looks this year. What’s being served: fashion as art.

In the three decades since red carpets have become synonymous with Hollywood couture, celebrity stylists have outpaced fashion editors, models, moguls and, more recently, content creators as the true arbiters of the town’s taste. No one else has the number of media impressions that top Hollywood stylists do, with many of them pulling in millions of followers. Of course, Beyoncé, Rihanna and Taylor Swift have 500 million-plus Instagram fans each, but much of the engagement is driven by what their stylists are putting on their backs.

That’s why, as this year winds down, THR reached out to the many pros who’ve now achieved fame in their own right for dressing the most visible personages in the world. What did we learn? The newish Parisian design duo behind Matières Fécales — Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran — have captured stylists’ hearts the most, while Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel, Jonathan Anderson’s Dior and Anthony Vaccarello’s Saint Laurent also number among Hollywood’s favorite designers. Feathers still are flying on red carpet fits for all genders. The sheer look continues to show off, but cutouts and two-piece looks are taking over the body-part wars. Lace, lingerie and leather are now completely red carpet-worthy. Slinky close fits and strong tailoring are forever. And so, apparently, is fashion’s idolization of Zendaya. We could have easily included three or more of her looks, but to keep the list varied and fun, we chose only one top fit per actor or actress. The methodology behind the list included tabulating the top 10 looks chosen by 50-plus stylists, prioritizing by the number of votes each look received, and then, to break ties, bringing in rankings. The result: a realistic look at coming trends and which designers and designs rank the highest for Hollywood, by the world’s top tastemakers.

At the NYC premiere of The Odyssey on July 14, America’s favorite zillennial stunned in Matières Fécales’ “Ange” gown. Styled by Law Roach, the micro-hand-pleated chiffon creation sported white rooster feather wings designed to evoke Zendaya’s character in the movie: Greek goddess Athena. “What I loved most about the Matières angel look,” says stylist Ilaria Urbinati (her clients: Dwayne Johnson, Barry Keoghan) “is how cohesively ethereal it felt from head to toe. It didn’t look costume-y. She looked like a painting. Not many could pull it off.” Adds stylist Tara Swennen (Kristen Stewart, Ali Wong), “It literally took my breath away.”

At the Met Gala on May 4, Chamberlain grabbed the limelight in custom Mugler by Miguel Castro Freitas. Inspired by impressionist painters, the one-of-a-kind rainbow dress, styled by Jared Ellner, took 40 hours to paint and four days to dry. “It really embodied the ‘Fashion Is Art’ Met Ball theme without feeling like a costume,” says stylist Tracy Shapoff (Molly Parker, Bill Maher). “The gorgeous hand-painting texture on the dress felt as though they’d painted a one-of-a-kind piece directly onto her body. I really felt like I was looking at a piece of artwork.”

Styled by Wayman + Micah, last Oscar season’s breakout Infiniti radiated in custom Thom Browne at the May 4 Met Gala. Made of 1.5 million hand-embroidered sequins and over 600 shades of silk fringe, the gown was inspired by the Greek sculpture of Venus de Milo. “There’s something surreal about it,” says stylist Avigail Collins (part of a team with husband Damian; they work with Elizabeth Olsen and St. Vincent). “Like wearable art, almost sculptural, the way the sequins, beading, intricate embroidery, craftsmanship and embellishments create an abstract silhouette, pushing the boundaries of fashion.”

Also wearing custom Thom Browne and also styled by Wayman + Micah, another of last awards season’s standouts, Taylor, grabbed fashion mindshare at the Actor Awards on March 1. The surrealist molded gown in gray and off-white was meant to evoke an abstract painting of a naked woman’s body, with ribbons dripping down the back. The “naked” anatomical bodice was made from over 160 pattern pieces put together via intarsia and tonal shading to mimic carved musculature; the gray tulle mermaid skirt was embellished with over 400,000 sequins in gold and white gold.

In a ruby-beaded, liquid-looking Chanel confection, Kidman, styled by Jason Bolden, turned heads at the Met Gala on May 4. Chanel’s Matthieu Blazy created the dropped-waist silhouette, with feathers at the hips and cuffs, a long dramatic train and surprising long sleeves. “What I loved most about that gown,” offers stylist James Yardley (Connor Storrie, Hannah Waddingham), “was its simplicity. Immaculate fit, and the placement of the feathers had such an impact. The cherry on top: the spinel and lapis lazuli ring, also from Chanel.”

Wearing this Miu Miu crystal corseted gown at the Oct. 1 Sydney premiere of Sense and Sensibility, Edgar-Jones, as styled by Dani Michelle, perfectly referenced Jane Austen’s era, with delicate ribbons as shoulder straps. “This strikes all the right notes,” declares stylist Ariel Tunnell (Rachel Bloom, Stephanie Beatriz). “The color, the sheer elements, the tones against her skin — so flattering. Add in the historical dressing of corsets and lacing, and it comes together in the coolest and most gorgeous way.”

Modelling custom Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello at the Sept. 27 MTV Video Music Awards and styled by Chris Horan, the music provocateur reminded that the midriff is an erogenous zone. Goth and glam at the same time, Charli embodied a modern Morticia Addams. “I can’t think of anyone who knows who they are better than Charli XCX,” stylist Michael Fisher tells THR (Ethan Hawke, Jon Hamm, Jake Gyllenhaal). “Every time I see her on a carpet, she’s perfectly herself and looks effortlessly cool.”

Styled by Jahleel Weaver, she wore a custom metallic architectural creation by Maison Margiela artistic director Glenn Martens for the May 4 Met Gala. Inspired by the medieval buildings of the Flanders region of Belgium, it was sewn from duchess silk, recycled metal threads and 115,000 crystal beads alongside antique jewels and chains. The label’s Paris atelier spent 1,380 hours of handwork on what Rihanna described as “looking like a pearl emerging from an oxidized oyster shell,” a reference to her home country of Barbados.

The Schiaparelli couture lace gown worn by the model multihyphenate and styled by Mimi Cuttrell for the Cannes Film Festival was an homage to Jane Birkin. It required 130 artisans to create. Stylist Molly Dickson (Sydney Sweeney, Kaia Gerber) offers: “Everything Daniel Roseberry does at Schiaparelli is incredible. This dress balances delicate proportions and contrast perfectly. The crochet is intricate; the V of the neck is the perfect line. And let’s not forget the back! It has a black ribbon corset lacing up to the neck, providing the tiniest bit of edge.”

Only badass Theron, as styled by Leslie Fremar, could sex up this suit from Dior men’s fall 2026 collection, which she wore to the April 22 NYC premiere of Apex. “This look stood out to me,” says stylist Lee Harris (Helen Mirren, Drew Barrymore), “because in this red carpet world in which so many try to go over the top for attention, this was razor sharp and clean, with just one powerful accessory. She wore the look — the look didn’t wear her.”

In Celine at a Good Morning America appearance in February promoting Love Story, Kelly wowed stylists and fashion luminaries of all genders. Styled by Warren Alfie Baker, the combo of jacket, rep tie and jeans hearkened back to his character, JFK Jr. “I love when well-worn denim makes its way into celeb dressing because it’s always unexpected,” says stylist Erica Cloud (Robert Downey Jr., Mia Goth). “The homage to JFK Jr. in the ’90s was a great intro to Paul’s fashion presence. The little Celine details — minimal loafers, squared-off tie — were icing on the cake.”

Swinton’s striking Chanel couture cocoon silhouette, complete with vertical pleating and a soft, body-conscious drape, was styled by Jerry Stafford for Cannes. Notes stylist Sarah Slutsky Tooley (Maya Hawke, Emma Watson, Elizabeth Olsen): “I’ve looked to Tilda as a style icon since I began in fashion. This look has unexpected proportions, matching tomato red with white kitten heels. It’s so thoughtful, though so easy. She looks so cool, completely refreshing and unexpected. Fashion is so natural to her DNA.”

At the Jan. 28 L.A. Wuthering Heights premiere, Elordi drew admiration as a very tall, masculine figure in a Chanel cropped jacket, all styled by Wendi and Nicole Ferreira. “This Chanel look masters understated luxury with a relaxed, modern twist,” notes stylist Chris Brown (David Beckham, Luke Evans, Leo Woodall). “The oversized blazer, soft knitwear and cream trousers create an elegant tonal palette, while the loose fit keeps things effortlessly modern. It’s a lesson in quiet confidence.”

In Erdem at the MTV Video Music Video Awards, Sivan sported tuxedo suiting with sharp shoulders and a stiff, upturned collar, but from the waist down was adorned with ostrich feathers and satin and tulle trim. Styled by Marc Forne, this look was adapted from an Erdem dress in the spring/summer 2027 collection that was inspired by 1920s American aerialist Barbette, who performed in drag. Erdem used that as a jumping-off point to play with masculine and feminine tropes, combining strict tailoring and dramatic stage costume.

In a custom pink, plush velvet double-breasted suit with flared pants by Louis Vuitton, Pharrell cut an appropriately high-fashion figure at the Feb. 1 Grammys. Styled by Matthew Henson, the Vuitton men’s creative director also made matching suits for Clipse — the hip-hop duo also known as Malice and Pusha T, who were named by Pharrell himself — for their Grammy-night reunion. Pharrell also donned two Jacob & Co. Georgian-style yellow and white diamond riviera necklaces and diamond stud earrings.

In an intricate Saint Laurent black-lace ballgown at the Met Gala, Hollywood’s perennial cool girl was in top form, as styled by Danielle Goldberg. “The silhouette creates a striking contrast between sleek sensuality and vintage drama,” comments stylist Brown. “It’s a look that feels mysterious, tactile and unapologetically individual, with Saint Laurent’s signature rock ’n’ roll attitude running throughout.” Kravitz’s Met Ball date was not her fiancé, Harry Styles, but one of her most-worn designers, Saint Laurent creative director Anthony Vaccarello.

In 36-year-old Turkish fashion designer Dilara Findikoglu at the Met Gala, Ortega played up her Goth character Wednesday Addams with a full-on peekaboo look, styled by Enrique Melendez. “I love that the chest is covered and the cutouts are on the sides of this gown,” says Dickson. “It’s like a reverse of the expected, creating an interesting moment on the carpet.”

Pairing a vintage John Galliano brocade feather-cuffed coat with a micro-mini and red tights for the Feb. 5 London premiere of Wuthering Heights, Robbie caught lightning. Styled by Andrew Mukamal, the head-to-toe look is a brilliant study in dissonance, pairing modern and Gothic. “What we loved about this look,” says stylist Avigail Collins, “was the contrast between the romance of the 1992 archival Galliano coat and the sexiness of the black mini, red stockings and that clashing pink ribbon. An unexpected combination that works beautifully.”

Styled by Nick Royal and Peri Rosenzweig of Hardstyle, the original little monster wore a black feathered gown with a train by Matières Fécales to the Grammys. “The cut sold me,” says stylist Nico Amarca (Atticus Ross, Chase Hudson). “Feathers go straight up the neck, lock around her jaw like armor, a hard look. Gaga’s biggest looks have always been about shock. This one was about control: one material, all black, no gimmick. Choosing a young, independent house like Matières Fécales over a legacy name made it even better.”

Donning a white Schiaparelli suit with broad-brimmed hat while marrying Callum Turner at a London civil wedding on May 31, the singer-songwriter struck a Lorenzo Posocco-styled iconic silhouette. THR artistic director Alison Edmond explains, “It was all the more stylish by the location being so low-key; I loved that for them. She owned that Bianca Jagger reference, but made it Dua: the suit, hat, gloves, pumps, the flowers — perfection. There’s so much reality (in the dictionary sense of the word) about this couple: real love, real bodies, real sexiness … no fake relationship here.”

Styled by Jamie Mizrahi, Pascal shone at the Academy Awards in a custom Chanel jacketless tuxedo shirt with a white floral brooch made of silk and feathers, as unconventional as an Oscar look can get. “A guide to how to be a stylish man in formal wear, without being garish,” says stylist Melendez (Jenna Ortega, Inde Navarrette). “He hit the perfect medium. The exquisite tuxedo shirt with flower brooch moment added subtle drama we love to see in a carpet look, and that we always appreciate in men’s styling. The accentuated waist with the cummerbund showcased the fine tailoring.”

Styled by Anastasia Walker and showcasing a cropped tux by Mexican designer Patricio Campillo, the country hip-hop star made quite an impression. “Shaboozey walked into the Oscars and turned black-tie into a full showman moment!” says stylist Chaise Dennis (Tramell Tillman, Edward Norton.) “It’s impeccably tailored, totally distinct, so much fun. He put on a show. I also love the support of a small brand like Campillo on such a big stage.”

The Jan. 11 Golden Globes was the first time J.Law went sheer. Styled by Ryan Hastings, the custom semi-transparent Givenchy gown was designed by Sarah Burton. “The look was both floral and sheer,” enthuses stylist Melendez, “which doesn’t sound too exciting until you actually see it! The perfectly placed appliqués made this look the perfect blend of sultry and sweet, and the addition of the silk embroidered shrug instantly made it even more captivating — an almost street-style element added in the most elevated way.”

The Khaite backless custom leather halter-neck gown at the Emmys, as worn by The Diplomat star Russell and styled by Frank Fleming, was one of a number of edgy appearances. Her accessories matched the toughened look: high black stilettos, Buccellati garnet and diamond gold jewelry, and a slicked back, low ballerina bun. “This is a perfect look,” notes Cloud. “Equal amounts of nonchalance and edgy sexiness.”

Moore was on the judging panel at the Cannes Film Festival, and her red carpet entrances encompassed 10 amazing looks styled by Brad Goreski, including this full-on ballgown by the provocative Paris duo of Matières Fécales. “A hot-pink Matières Fécales gown at Cannes, before most people knew the brand — perfect irreverence,” says stylist Britt Mccamey (Tracee Ellis Ross, Sadie Sink). “I respect how much Demi and Brad care about art in fashion. No algorithm could have picked this for her, that was the whole point. It’s fun to have fun!”

“I enjoyed the detailing of this look,” says stylist Chloe Takayanagi (Sterling K. Brown, Kumail Nanjiani) of the details on Jordan’s custom-tailored Louis Vuitton Nehru-collar suit, styled by Jason Bolden for the Oscars. “I loved the brooch on the back of the neck and the watch chains, which seemed like a light nod to his character in Sinners. The mandarin, stand collar jacket was also a refreshing take on a classic-cut suit.”

Styled by Karla Welch, Reinsve wore a number of Louis Vuitton dresses throughout awards season, all of them stark and revealing at the same time. The one she wore to the Oscars was a red strapless column gown with a sweeping train. “This was one of my favorite looks of Renate’s, the simplest dress, so effortless,” describes stylist Jessica Paster (Emily Blunt, Quinta Brunson). “It’s a beautiful dress — the sleekness of the slit up the leg — and the color. Sooo chic.”

“I adored seeing Malkovich walk down the carpet in this look in Venice,” says THR’s Edmond of the actor’s Dior suit at the film festival. “He has a touch of the genius in his work, and stylist Jeanne Yang is certainly talented enough to know how to showcase the theatrical via the sartorial. The beautifully oversized suit with the tied and pleated collar: What a perfect mix of fashion and film, putting Jonathan Anderson’s flourishes on this incredible actor.”

The corsetry and exaggerated shape of Pugh’s Vivienne Westwood at the Sept. 30 NYC premiere of East of Eden strongly references her character’s early 20th century wardrobe. “This is the power of a strong silhouette,” observes Swennen of stylist Rebecca Corbin-Murray’s work. “The volume’s deliberate, yet does not overwhelm her. The fabric is so regal and opulent and the color — lime green/chartreuse — that’s something you don’t see often on the red carpet. I love it when people take risks, when they’re bold. It’s a very regal, luxurious look.”

#712. Nicolas Cage Weighs in on Ryan Gosling’s Ghost Rider, 20 Years After His Version

"I was happy for him and wished him best of luck on his adventures and I look forward to seeing the movie," Cage said of passing the fiery baton.

Nicolas Cage is endorsing Ryan Gosling‘s upcoming take on Ghost Rider, nearly two decades after he played the character.

Cage starred in 2007’s Ghost Rider, following motorcycle stuntman Johnny Blaze who sells his soul to become a bounty hunter of evil demons; he reprised the role in 2012 sequel Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance. Fast forward to this year, and Marvel announced at Comic-Con that Gosling would be leading a new Ghost Rider film, directed by Shawn Levy.

At the premiere of his new movie Madden, Cage weighed in on the new adaptation, telling The Hollywood Reporter, “Ryan’s going to do his thing with it and I’m looking forward to seeing it. Ryan knows how I feel about him as an actor; we’ve had nice conversations and we stay in touch. I was happy for him and wished him best of luck on his adventures and I look forward to seeing the movie.” Related Stories General News Nicolas Cage Says He's "a Little Bit Homeless" After Sinkhole Damaged His Malibu Home Lifestyle GQ Expands Men of the Year Footprint in L.A.

During the Comic-Con announcement in July, Gosling emphasized, “This is a character I’ve wanted to play for a very long time.” There is an additional layer as well, as Gosling’s wife Eva Mendes appeared alongside Cage in the original 2007 film; she has also supported her husband in taking over the fiery character.

The new Ghost Rider project is currently dated for July 28, 2028, and in addition to Gosling, Heated Rivalry breakout Connor Storrie is in talks to star as the film’s villain.

As for Cage, he is currently playing John Madden in David O. Russell‘s new film Madden, following the football icon and his relationship with Raiders owner Al Davis. Madden is hitting limited theaters on Nov. 11 and starts streaming Nov. 18 on Prime Video.

#711. Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders

Fire salamanders are among Europe's most recognizable amphibians, known for their striking black and yellow coloring and the poisonous substances they release to deter predators. Despite their familiar appearance, scientists are still uncovering surprising details about their biology. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies the species as "vulnerable" on its Red List of Threatened Species. Fire salamanders typically inhabit damp forests, streams, and mountainous regions, where habitat destruction and fragmentation increasingly threaten their survival.

New research has revealed that fire salamanders possess an unexpected ability to fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The glow is most pronounced on the yellow underside of their bodies and along their sides. Researchers traced the fluorescence primarily to glands in the animals' skin and the substances those glands release. Remarkably, these secretions can remain fluorescent for more than 24 hours after leaving the salamander's body.

"It is fascinating that such a well-studied species still harbors unknown phenomena like this. It reminds us that even the most familiar organisms can hide secrets that are only revealed when they are observed with new tools," says Bernat Burriel, a researcher at the Museum of Natural Sciences in Barcelona and the study's first author.

The phenomenon occurs when compounds in the salamander's skin absorb ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see, and reemit that energy as visible light. This process produces vivid green and cyan colors. Known as biofluorescence, it requires an outside source of illumination and should not be confused with bioluminescence. Animals such as fireflies produce their own light through chemical reactions, while fluorescent organisms must first absorb light from their surroundings.

Scientists once believed that biofluorescence occurred almost exclusively in marine organisms, with scorpions standing out as an unusual example on land. More recent studies have challenged that assumption, identifying fluorescent properties in a growing variety of terrestrial animals, including reptiles, birds, and amphibians.

Although researchers have confirmed that fire salamanders fluoresce, the biological purpose of this ability remains uncertain. One possibility is that the glow serves as a form of communication, helping individuals recognize one another or assess potential mates. Another is that it makes their warning coloration more noticeable to predators.

"Fluorescence meets several criteria that suggest a communicative function. It could help salamanders detect each other in nocturnal or particularly dense environments, or act as an additional defense signal," says Martin Kaltenpoth, director of the Department of Insect Symbiosis at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-author of the study.

The discovery that toxic skin secretions are also fluorescent raises additional questions about how salamanders interact with predators and other animals in their environment.

For now, these proposed functions remain hypotheses. Animals with particularly sensitive vision may be able to detect the green and cyan fluorescence even when it is extremely faint. Humans, however, need a UV lamp to observe the effect.

In the forests where fire salamanders live, nighttime illumination comes primarily from moonlight and starlight. Researchers note that full moonlight contains a greater proportion of ultraviolet and violet wavelengths than daylight, which has a more evenly distributed spectrum. Under these conditions, fluorescence could create small green and cyan highlights against the salamanders' yellow markings, potentially making them easier for other salamanders to spot.

Could the Fluorescent Glow Warn Predators?

Another possible explanation involves aposematism, a defensive strategy in which animals display conspicuous colors to advertise that they are poisonous or otherwise dangerous. Fire salamanders already use their distinctive yellow and black patterns as warning signals, and fluorescence might provide an additional visual cue.

Scientists established a connection between salamander warning colors and chemical defenses more than a century ago when they identified samandarines. These highly toxic steroidal alkaloids are produced from cholesterol precursors and contribute to the animals' chemical protection.

Despite decades of research into salamander toxins and skin chemistry, the newly observed fluorescence came as a surprise.

"The presence of this fluorescent compound was surprising because salamander skin secretions have been studied chemically for decades, and we were unaware of any published reports on fluorescence," says Andrés Brunetti, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-first author of the study.

One of the biggest unanswered questions concerns the substance responsible for the fluorescence. Researchers have not yet determined its chemical identity, although the evidence suggests it may be a molecule not previously recognized in fire salamanders.

"We still don't know what the compound responsible for this fluorescence is, but everything indicates that it is a molecule unknown until now in this species. Identifying it will be key to understanding its origin and function," adds Salvador Carranza, a researcher at the IBE (CSIC-UPF) and another co-author of the study.

The team is now working to identify and chemically characterize potential compounds responsible for the effect. Determining which molecule produces the glow could help explain how the fluorescence develops and whether it plays a meaningful role in salamander behavior or survival.

A New Discovery With Implications for Amphibian Conservation

Beyond revealing an unexpected feature of a familiar species, the findings demonstrate how new research techniques can uncover biological traits that have escaped scientific attention for decades.

Understanding whether fluorescence influences communication, mating, or predator avoidance could also contribute to conservation efforts. Such information may help researchers better understand the behavior and ecological needs of fire salamanders, which already face significant threats from habitat loss and fragmentation.

The research also involved scientists from the Institute of Subtropical Biology and the Catalan Society of Herpetology. It forms part of a pioneering amphibian conservation project in Catalonia supported by the Barcelona Zoo Foundation.

Grab your high-lumen flashlight and gargantuan gun to explore these vicious vessels

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Abandoned, possessed, or infested spaceships in sci-fi films, books, and video games are usually not a welcoming place to hang your helmet and kick back inside.

Many are distinctly marked as DO NOT APPROACH zones and equipped with clearly articulated warning messages to keep your distance, but that doesn't ever seem to stop scavengers, space pirates, or evil industrial mega corporations from waving off these dangerous signs to board anyway.

Other creaky craft are apt to contain nasty alien hitchhikers or biological hazards not exactly conducive to a pleasant star-trekking voyage. Whether these nefarious neglected craft have just reappeared from the other side of a black hole or have been lying dormant for eons on a hostile planetoid, visitors are usually infrequent.

So ignore those distress beacons at your own peril and step into this alarming armada of 9 nightmarish sci-fi spaceships before orbits decay.

This is not a ranked list, just a collection of our favorites.

It's basically a perfectly good interstellar mining vessel owned by the Concordance Extraction Corporation if you forget about the nasty reanimated corpses found lurking on nearly every deadly deck.

The pesky Necromorphs are a resilient crop of creatures and are extremely inhospitable when it comes to having uninvited guests, yet they don't mind if you're staying for dinner.

This plague of hungry zombified corpses is a real drag, unless you happen to have a flaring plasma cutter in your back pocket and your name is Isaac Clarke.

Things would be much more peaceful aboard the Grendel if a notorious undead slasher named Jason Voorhees wasn't stashed in the cargo bay, but when scientific discovery enters the equation, many questionable choices follow.

The Grendel is a 25th-century medical research vessel on a field trip from hell to an overly polluted Earth, where the frozen Jason is kept at the Crystal Lake Research Facility and shipped back home to Earth 2 for cellular research.

Once thawed, the ship becomes his private killing field with an ample supply of student bodies until the fiery finale when Jason becomes an inhuman meteor in the sky. Next time, take the school bus.

This spooky classic novel written by "2001's" legendary author, Arthur C. Clarke, focuses on a massive alien spaceship entering Earth's atmosphere.

The 31-mile-long cylindrical spaceship does not parallel park easily and is quite spacious inside. In fact, it’s primarily hollow at first and likely offers up a fantastic location for some echoey yodeling. As we later learn, Rama aliens are apparently collecting forms of intelligent life from around the galaxy, employing their ginormous Rama spacecraft.

As an ice ring thaws and forms a vast ocean, astronauts explore the ship’s cavernous confines, only to find automated bio-machines and weird metallic towers, curved alloy cliffs, and fantastic geometric city-like structures. The myriad mysteries that unfold are enough to drive sane humans to absolute madness!

Ignore that glistening brown protomolecular goo, and come on in and sit a spell in the Scopuli, a light Martian freighter used by the Outer Planets Alliance for clandestine missions and ransacked by the evil security firm Protogen in an attempt to hijack its alien cargo.

Hailing from James S.A. Corey's first book in "The Expanse Series", the Scopuli was found moored to an asteroid by James Holden and his Canterbury crew. The amber-brown mess discovered inside the rigged ship is not to be trifled with, let alone inhaled, eaten, or touched.

Come to think of it, it’s probably much wiser to get out while you can and move along!

Anything that looks like an organic hammer-headed horseshoe lying canted in a rocky ravine on a hostile, uncharted planetoid is best to avoid. Especially when its repeating SOS beacon is translated into its true message… a dire warning to keep curious rubberneckers the hell away!

Once its strange, sexually suggestive openings are penetrated by Nostromo crew members, seeing fossilized giants and oceans of squishy egg pods in the cargo hold would make most reasonable people flee in terror.

We're better off leaving this sleeping nightmare in its resting place.

One of the inspirations for Ridley Scott's "Alien", this Golden Age goodie brings us aboard the sleek silver rescue rocketship, Challenge 142, and locks us inside after a bloodthirsty reptilian alien from Mars decides to catch a lift back to Earth with its new astronaut friends in the far-flung future of... 1973!

Mute, clawed monsters with insatiable appetites for human flesh are never good travel companions in the confines of a steel spacecraft. A wiser choice would have been to have stayed on Mars and used the Challenge 142 as a stylized red planet potato farm.

Need a glowing golden suntan? This vessel was launched from Earth to detonate a nuclear payload within the sun's fury to keep its fusion furnace burning and was never heard from again.

A sister rescue vessel, the Icarus 2, was dispatched as a last resort and encountered this long-abandoned ship drifting near the scorching star. Inside the Icarus 1, its over-tanned Captain Pinback has been caught in an addictive ritual of basking in the sun's brilliant embrace and has gone quite insane.

Back out quietly and toss him a nice bottle of aloe vera lotion.

Lawrence Fishburne's Captain Miller thinks this place is a tomb! Well, that's not a very polite way to describe what I think is one of the most ominous spaceships ever seen on screen.

The fact that this foreboding vessel, designed after the cathedral of Notre Dame, has appeared in Neptune's orbit following its disappearance after entering a black hole should be enough to keep the crew of the Lewis and Clark from steering anywhere close. Nothing good can be happening on that doomed craft considering the seven-year absence.

One second after discovering that the craft punctured a route straight to Hades and returned with some extra baggage, I'd be running for the exit hatch! The welcome mat is out, but there's no need to knock on this airlock.

Basically an "Alien" ripoff, this low-budget cult sci-fi flick has its following, but only from those midnight runs to the video store in the '80s to grab the tape with the craziest-looking alien on the cover.

The Shenandoah is a prospecting explorer sent by a ruthless corporation to claim an alien archaeological site on Saturn's moon, Titan. Assorted chaos ensues when a rival West German spaceship is discovered at the dig site, only for our protagonists to find the crew slaughtered.

The carnivorous monster that creeps onto the Shenandoah suffers from little monster syndrome, but its bite is impressive. Best to have never touched the metallic pods in the subterranean cave and just skipped this homicidal mission entirely.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.
